description: This topic covers the formation, preparation and properties of common metal compounds: oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates, nitrates, chlorides and sulphates. It links each type of salt to the acid used to prepare it, explains thermal decomposition reactions, and highlights the industrial importance of compounds such as limestone and copper(II) sulphate.

mcq.questionText: A compound formed when a metal combines with oxygen is called a metal:
mcq.explanation: When a metal combines with oxygen it forms a metal oxide. Exam Tip: Metal oxides are generally basic (e.g. MgO, CaO) and react with acids to form salts.

mcq.questionText: Metal oxides generally react with acids to produce:

options.text: A salt and hydrogen gas only

mcq.explanation: This is a neutralisation-type reaction, giving a salt and water. Exam Tip: Metal oxide + acid -> salt + water. E.g. CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O.

mcq.questionText: A compound containing the hydroxide (OH-) radical combined with a metal is called a metal:
mcq.explanation: A metal combined with the hydroxide radical forms a metal hydroxide. Exam Tip: Soluble metal hydroxides are alkalis (e.g. NaOH, KOH); many are also insoluble bases (e.g. Cu(OH)2).

mcq.questionText: Metal carbonates react with dilute acids to produce a salt, water and:
mcq.explanation: Metal carbonate plus acid releases carbon dioxide, along with a salt and water. Exam Tip: Metal carbonate + acid -> salt + water + carbon dioxide. CO2 turns limewater milky, confirming the gas.

mcq.questionText: Heating a metal carbonate (thermal decomposition) generally produces:

options.text: A metal oxide and carbon dioxide

mcq.explanation: Heat decomposes a metal carbonate into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide gas. Exam Tip: E.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (heating limestone to make quicklime).

options.text: Insoluble in water and very stable to heat
Soluble in water and decompose easily on heating

mcq.explanation: Metal hydrogen carbonates tend to be more soluble and less stable to heat than the corresponding carbonates. Exam Tip: Sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda, NaHCO3) is a common, soluble, heat-sensitive example.

mcq.questionText: Metal nitrates are generally prepared by reacting a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with:
mcq.explanation: Reacting with nitric acid (HNO3) forms nitrate salts. Exam Tip: Match the acid to the salt: nitric acid -> nitrates; sulphuric acid -> sulphates; hydrochloric acid -> chlorides.

mcq.questionText: On strong heating, most metal nitrates decompose to release oxygen and:

options.text: A brown gas (nitrogen dioxide) and the metal oxide

mcq.explanation: Many metal nitrates decompose to the metal oxide, releasing brown nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen. Exam Tip: The brown fumes (NO2) are a distinctive sign of decomposing metal nitrates on heating.

mcq.questionText: Metal chlorides are generally prepared by reacting a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with:
mcq.explanation: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) produces chloride salts. Exam Tip: Chloride comes from hydrochloric acid. Match the acid's name to the salt's name.

mcq.questionText: Common salt (sodium chloride) is an example of a metal:
mcq.explanation: NaCl is a chloride (sodium and chlorine, from hydrochloric acid neutralisation). Exam Tip: NaCl (table salt) is the everyday example of a metal chloride.

mcq.questionText: Metal sulphates are generally prepared by reacting a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with:
mcq.explanation: Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) produces sulphate salts. Exam Tip: Sulphate comes from sulphuric acid. Learn all three acid-salt pairs: HCl -> chloride, H2SO4 -> sulphate, HNO3 -> nitrate.

options.text: Colourless and odourless with no water content
Blue in colour, containing water of crystallisation

mcq.explanation: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate crystals are blue, containing water molecules within the crystal structure. Exam Tip: Heating blue hydrated CuSO4 drives off the water, leaving white anhydrous CuSO4, a classic reversible test for water.

mcq.questionText: Metal compounds such as carbonates and hydroxides are important in industry for making:

options.text: Paints, drinking water treatment, soaps and detergents

mcq.explanation: Metal compounds are raw materials for paints, water treatment chemicals, soaps and detergents. Exam Tip: Metal compounds are far more than laboratory curiosities, they underpin many everyday industries.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a use of calcium carbonate (limestone)?
mcq.explanation: Limestone (CaCO3) is a raw material for cement and glass manufacture. Exam Tip: Limestone is also heated to make quicklime (CaO), used to treat acidic soils.

mcq.questionText: Which pair correctly matches the acid used to prepare each type of metal salt?

options.text: HCl gives sulphate; H2SO4 gives chloride
HCl gives chloride; H2SO4 gives sulphate; HNO3 gives nitrate
HNO3 gives chloride; HCl gives nitrate
All acids give the same salt

mcq.explanation: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) gives chloride; sulphuric acid (H2SO4) gives sulphate; nitric acid (HNO3) gives nitrate. Exam Tip: The salt name usually matches the acid's ending: chloric acid -> chloride; sulphuric acid -> sulphate; nitric acid -> nitrate.

fib.questionText: A compound formed when a metal combines with oxygen is called a metal ____.
fib.explanation: A metal combined with oxygen forms a metal oxide. Exam Tip: E.g. MgO, CuO, CaO.

fib.questionText: A compound containing a metal combined with the OH- radical is called a metal ____.
fib.explanation: A metal combined with the hydroxide radical forms a metal hydroxide. Exam Tip: E.g. NaOH, Ca(OH)2.

fib.questionText: Heating a metal carbonate produces a metal ____ and carbon dioxide.
fib.explanation: Thermal decomposition of a carbonate produces the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. Exam Tip: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating.

fib.questionText: Metal chlorides are prepared using ____ acid.
fib.explanation: Hydrochloric acid is the acid used to prepare chloride salts. Exam Tip: HCl gives chloride salts.

fib.questionText: Metal sulphates are prepared using ____ acid.
fib.explanation: Sulphuric acid is the acid used to prepare sulphate salts. Exam Tip: H2SO4 gives sulphate salts.

fib.questionText: Metal nitrates are prepared using ____ acid.
fib.explanation: Nitric acid is the acid used to prepare nitrate salts. Exam Tip: HNO3 gives nitrate salts.

fib.questionText: On strong heating, most metal nitrates release oxygen, the metal oxide, and a brown gas called ____.
fib.explanation: The brown gas released when metal nitrates decompose is nitrogen dioxide. Exam Tip: Brown fumes (NO2) confirm a metal nitrate is decomposing.

fib.questionText: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate crystals are ____ in colour.
fib.explanation: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate is blue. Exam Tip: Heating turns it white (anhydrous); adding water turns it blue again.

fib.questionText: Limestone is chemically known as calcium ____.
fib.explanation: Limestone is chemically calcium carbonate. Exam Tip: CaCO3 equals calcium carbonate equals limestone.

fib.questionText: Metal carbonates react with dilute acids to release carbon dioxide gas, water and a ____.
fib.explanation: The third product of a metal carbonate reacting with an acid is a salt. Exam Tip: Metal carbonate + acid -> salt + water + CO2.

tf.questionText: A metal oxide is a compound formed when a metal combines with oxygen.
tf.explanation: This is the correct definition of a metal oxide. Metal oxides are generally basic in nature.

tf.questionText: Metal oxides react with acids to produce a gas and no salt.
tf.explanation: Metal oxide plus acid produces a salt and water, not a gas. A gas is released with carbonates plus acid, not oxides.

tf.questionText: Metal carbonates react with acids to release carbon dioxide gas.
tf.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a product of this reaction and turns limewater milky, confirming it.

tf.questionText: Heating limestone (calcium carbonate) produces calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
tf.explanation: CaCO3 decomposes on heating to CaO + CO2, an industrial process that makes quicklime.

tf.questionText: Metal hydrogen carbonates are generally more stable to heat than metal carbonates.
tf.explanation: Hydrogen carbonates are generally less stable and decompose more easily than the corresponding carbonates.

tf.questionText: Metal chlorides are prepared using hydrochloric acid.
tf.explanation: Reacting a metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with HCl gives the chloride salt.

tf.questionText: Metal sulphates are prepared using nitric acid.
tf.explanation: Sulphates come from sulphuric acid, not nitric acid; nitric acid gives nitrates.

tf.questionText: Most metal nitrates decompose on strong heating, releasing a brown gas.
tf.explanation: Brown nitrogen dioxide gas is typically released when metal nitrates decompose on heating.

tf.questionText: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate is white, while anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is blue.
tf.explanation: The colours are the opposite way round: hydrated copper(II) sulphate is blue, while anhydrous is white.

tf.questionText: Limestone (calcium carbonate) is used industrially in making cement and glass.
tf.explanation: Limestone is a key raw material in cement and glass production.

summary.correctAnswer: A compound formed when a metal combines with oxygen, such as MgO or CuO; generally basic and reacts with acids to form a salt and water.
summary.explanation: Metal oxide + acid -> salt + water, with no gas released.

summary.correctAnswer: A compound formed when a metal combines with the hydroxide (OH-) radical, such as NaOH or Ca(OH)2.
summary.explanation: Soluble metal hydroxides are alkalis, while many others are insoluble bases.

summary.correctAnswer: A compound containing a metal combined with the carbonate (CO3 2-) radical; reacts with acids to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide, and decomposes on heating to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
summary.explanation: Carbon dioxide gas from this reaction turns limewater milky, a key diagnostic test.

summary.correctAnswer: A compound containing a metal, hydrogen and the carbonate radical, such as sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3); generally more soluble and less stable to heat than the corresponding carbonate.
summary.explanation: Sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) decomposes at a lower temperature than sodium carbonate.

summary.correctAnswer: A salt formed when a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate reacts with nitric acid; most decompose on strong heating to give the metal oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen.
summary.explanation: The brown fumes released on heating are a distinctive test for a metal nitrate.

summary.correctAnswer: A salt formed when a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid, for example sodium chloride (common salt).
summary.explanation: The acid's name (hydrochloric) matches the salt's name (chloride).

summary.correctAnswer: A salt formed when a metal, its oxide, hydroxide or carbonate reacts with sulphuric acid, for example copper(II) sulphate.
summary.explanation: The acid's name (sulphuric) matches the salt's name (sulphate).

summary.correctAnswer: Water molecules chemically combined within the crystal structure of a compound, such as in blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate.
summary.explanation: Heating drives off this water, turning blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate into white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate.

summary.correctAnswer: The breaking down of a compound into two or more simpler substances using heat, for example CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
summary.explanation: Heating a metal carbonate is a classic example of thermal decomposition tested in exams.

summary.correctAnswer: Calcium oxide (CaO), produced by strongly heating (thermally decomposing) limestone (calcium carbonate); used to treat acidic soils and in cement-making.
summary.explanation: Quicklime is a real-world application linking the carbonate decomposition reaction to agriculture and industry.

hoq.questionText: A student is given an unlabelled white powder and asked to determine whether it is a metal carbonate. She adds dilute hydrochloric acid and observes bubbling; she then passes the gas produced through limewater, which turns milky. Explain the observations and identify the type of compound.

options.text: The powder is a metal oxide; the gas is oxygen
The powder is a metal carbonate; the bubbling is carbon dioxide gas being released, confirmed by the limewater turning milky, from the reaction: carbonate + acid -> salt + water + carbon dioxide
The powder is a metal chloride; no gas should form
The powder is a metal nitrate; the gas is nitrogen dioxide

hoq.explanation: Bubbling with acid and gas turning limewater milky matches the standard diagnostic test for a carbonate: carbonate + acid -> salt + water + carbon dioxide. Metal oxides react with acid without releasing gas, which is the key difference used to identify the compound type. Exam Tip: Bubbles with acid plus gas turning limewater milky is the standard diagnostic test for a CARBONATE.

hoq.questionText: A jeweller wants to prepare silver chloride, silver sulphate and silver nitrate for different uses. Identify which acid should be used for each preparation, and explain the general pattern.

options.text: Use hydrochloric acid for the chloride, sulphuric acid for the sulphate, and nitric acid for the nitrate, because each salt's name matches the acid used to make it
Use the same acid for all three
Use only nitric acid for everything
Acids are not involved in preparing these salts

hoq.explanation: Silver chloride needs hydrochloric acid, silver sulphate needs sulphuric acid, and silver nitrate needs nitric acid; the salt's name always matches the acid used. Exam Tip: This name-matching pattern (chloric to chloride, sulphuric to sulphate, nitric to nitrate) is a reliable shortcut for predicting which acid makes which salt, across any metal, not just silver.

hoq.questionText: A quarry produces limestone (calcium carbonate). Explain what happens when the limestone is strongly heated in a kiln, name the products, and describe ONE industrial use for the resulting product.

options.text: Limestone melts into a liquid with no chemical change
Limestone thermally decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; the calcium oxide (quicklime) produced is used to neutralise acidic soils in agriculture (or in cement-making)
Limestone turns into calcium chloride and hydrogen
Nothing happens to limestone when heated

hoq.explanation: Strong heating causes thermal decomposition, not melting: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, producing calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide gas. Calcium oxide is a base widely used to neutralise acidic soils in farming (and in cement manufacture). Exam Tip: Heating a carbonate is one of the most tested reactions in this topic: metal carbonate -> metal oxide + carbon dioxide, and linking the product to a real use shows its practical importance.
